tagline.text: Walk into three limestone caves at Bulwang, in the caves capital of the Philippines

location.label: Location
location.text: Bulwang Caves information center, Highway 6, Mabinay, Negros Oriental

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–2,000 (round-trip day trip from Dumaguete, per person)

children.text: Mabinay is a karst area in Negros Oriental with more than 100 known caves. Most visitors go to the Bulwang Caves information center, where a guide leads them on foot through three caves (Panligawan, Pandalihan and Crystal) in about 2 hours.

Mabinay is a small inland town in central Negros, known among Philippine cave lovers as the "Caves Capital of the Philippines." A wide belt of limestone means more than 100 caves are known, and locals say there may be as many as 400, though some accounts say only about a quarter of them have been identified. The town lies about
87km
northwest of Dumaguete, roughly
2 hours
by road depending on conditions, and adds a different kind of day to a beach-focused Negros trip.
The caves became widely known after a team of Dutch and Belgian speleologists explored them in 1989–1990. The longest cave they recorded is Odloman Cave, at
. Cayaso Cave, at

, is ranked ninth longest in the country. These large caves require rappelling or swimming through an underground river, so they are for experts and not regular tourist destinations. Locals also say villagers sheltered in the underground passages during the Japanese occupation, which suggests residents knew the caves long before the 1989 exploration. About half of the known caves are said to have been identified on that expedition.

Ordinary visitors go to the Bulwang Caves information center on Highway 6. After paying the entrance fee and hiring an accredited guide, you can walk through three caves, Panligawan, Pandalihan and Crystal, in about
2 hours
. All three caves are locked behind gates, so you cannot enter without a guide, and the electric lighting, steel walkways and railings inside make the visit possible without special equipment.

The routes inside are short and well kept, but the floor is wet and slippery, some sections are narrow, and the caves are difficult for visitors with disabilities. In return you get a close look at cave life such as bats, crickets, millipedes up to 25 cm long and tailless whip scorpions, along with formations like stalactites and stalagmites. The fees and hours in this guide come from 2025 data, so check with the information center before you go. The landscape was shaped by acidic rainwater dissolving limestone over hundreds of thousands of years, and guides sometimes mention that the island sits on small plates known as the Philippine Mobile Belt. With that explanation, the caves feel less like dark holes and more like a geology museum built over a very long time.
This is the first stop, a short, nearly horizontal cave about

long. Its name means "courtship," and halfway through, a collapsed ceiling forms a karst window that lets light in. The Ati, the indigenous people of Negros, are said to have visited it to ask the nature spirits for blessings. The light from the window shows the interior most clearly, which makes it a good spot for photos.
Considered the highlight of the three, this cave is about

long. It has many speleothems such as stalactites and stalagmites, along with some gypsum, though they are not true crystals. Oils from human hands stop the formations from growing, so do not touch them.

This is the last stop and was once mined for bat guano. Pseudoscorpions, crickets and a colony of bats live here. In the dark sections, follow your guide and watch your footing. It is polite not to shine your light at the ceiling for long, so the bats are not disturbed.

Large millipedes up to 25 cm long spray a purple liquid when touched, and it stains skin. You may also see tailless whip scorpions and frogs. Bats and birds are said to only visit and do not live permanently in these caves.

Odloman and Mambajo caves require rappelling from the entrance or swimming through an underground river, so they are for experienced cavers. Public access is reportedly restricted to protect the environment. Ordinary visitors are safest sticking to the three caves at Bulwang. Getting all the way through a single cave takes rope skills, equipment and an experienced guide.
This spring in the town center is the water source for the poblacion (town proper). It is a
3–5 minutes
ride from the town center by tricycle, jeepney or bus, and visitors swim, kayak and picnic here. Local folklore says the spring was formed by the tears of Binay, a woman grieving a lost love.
These caves were formed as acidic rainwater dissolved the limestone over hundreds of thousands of years. Mabinay sits inland at an average elevation of
, so it is slightly cooler than the coast. Walking through with a guide who explains all this is far more interesting.

items.title: Day trip from Dumaguete
items.subtitle: Three Bulwang caves and Mabinay Spring

children.text: Board a Ceres bus bound for Bacolod at the Dumaguete bus terminal. Tell the driver or conductor in advance that you are getting off at "Bulwang Caves."

Arrive at the Bulwang Caves information center, pay the entrance fee and get an accredited guide. You will receive a helmet and a lamp, but the lamps are reported to be poor quality, so bring your own headlamp if you can.
Start with Panligawan Cave. Take photos at the window where the collapsed ceiling lets light in, then visit Crystal Cave and Pandalihan Cave in turn.
After the roughly 2-hour tour, have a snack and lunch near the information center. Restaurants nearby are limited, so it is safer to bring a packed lunch or snacks.
Take a tricycle or bus into Mabinay town and rest your feet at Mabinay Spring.
Catch a bus back to Dumaguete. Check the last departure time locally.
This is a day trip that covers only the caves. The round trip from Dumaguete takes a long time, so an early start is important.
Arrive in Dumaguete, walk along Rizal Boulevard, and have dinner at a local restaurant while confirming the next day's plan.
Take an early bus to the Bulwang Caves information center in Mabinay and tour the three caves with a guide.
Rest at Mabinay Spring, then take an afternoon bus back to Dumaguete to relax or move on to your next destination.
Mabinay can be done as a round trip in one day, but the long travel time makes it a tight schedule, so allow some margin.
Fly nonstop from Manila (NAIA) to Dumaguete-Sibulan Airport (DGT) on Philippine Airlines or Cebu Pacific. The flight takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
From the airport, take a taxi or tricycle to downtown Dumaguete.
At the Dumaguete bus terminal, take a Ceres bus bound for Bacolod and get off at "Bulwang Caves." Mabinay is reported to be about
87km
and
2 hours
away.
Fares and first and last departure times change, so check at the terminal.
From the Mabinay bus terminal, a tricycle to Bulwang is reported to take about
20 minutes
. The Bulwang information center is about
10km
south of Mabinay town along Highway 6.
From Bacolod, the town is about
128km
away by Ceres bus.
If you drive a rental car or motorbike from Dumaguete, just follow the highway, but first consider whether you are comfortable on mountain roads.
Weather affects the caves more than the season does. Parts of the caves connect to groundwater, so access may be limited after heavy rain, and it is safest to check with the information center.
According to 2025 data, the Bulwang Caves are open all year from Monday to Saturday,
. They are reported to be closed on Sundays, so do not plan a visit for that day.

For a day round trip from Dumaguete, bus times are the biggest variable. The easiest plan is to leave early, finish the caves by late morning, and rest at Mabinay Spring in the afternoon before heading back.

Mabinay town has few places to stay, so most visitors make a day trip from Dumaguete. Dumaguete has plenty of hotels and restaurants, so it is easiest to stay a night there and plan around it. If you want to stay in Mabinay, contact the local tourism office or a guesthouse in advance.
There are few restaurants near the caves, so bring your own water and snacks. For lunch, you can eat at a local restaurant in Mabinay town or return to Dumaguete.
Mabinay is inland, with an average elevation of
and a range from
to

, so it is cooler than coastal cities. A light jacket is handy if you spend the evening in town. Motorcycle taxis (habal-habal), tricycles and jeepneys run around town, so getting around is not difficult.
Check with the Bulwang Caves information center (phone +63-926-973-9386) before your visit to confirm that it is open.
Some sections are slippery, so wear sturdy sneakers or hiking shoes with firm soles. Sandals are not recommended.
The lamps provided are reported to be weak, so bring a headlamp and spare batteries.
Large millipedes spray a purple liquid that stains skin when touched, so do not handle them.
Do not touch stalactites and stalagmites, because the oils from your hands stop them from growing.
Bring water and snacks, and remember that the caves are closed on Sundays.
Photography is allowed, but because it is dark, a bright phone light works better than a flash.
Do not try expert caves such as Odloman and Mambajo on your own as an ordinary traveler.
Large caves other than the three at Bulwang are for experts and require rappelling or swimming through an underground river, and no cave can be entered without a guide.
It is dark and the floor is wet and slippery inside, so walk slowly and follow your guide's instructions.
Caves are dark, enclosed spaces, so think carefully if you are claustrophobic.
The facilities are difficult for visitors with disabilities to access.
Cave conditions can change on days of heavy rain, so follow the information center's advice.
Fees and hours can change, so check the latest announcements.
After visiting the Mabinay caves, return to this base city with its hotels and restaurants for a rest. It is about
2 hours
away by bus.
